## Step 0 — Scope challenge

**Already-solved sub-problems the plan should lean on harder:**

| Need | Already exists |
|---|---|
| `SidebarID` ⟷ persisted string | `AppStore.targetIDString(for:)` / `sidebarID(forTargetID:in:)` — `nonisolated static`, unit-tested |
| Terminal-excluding projection of `TabContent` | **`NavPayload`** (`Core/NavigationHistory.swift:53`) with both bridges already written (`TerminalSessions.swift:138`, `:157`) |
| Leaf-drop + collapse semantics | `PaneLayout.removingLeaf` (`Models/PaneLayout.swift:120`) |
| Restore-pending plumbing | `pendingRestoreSelection` (`AppStore.swift:839` → `:2495`) |
| Tab construction with a title | `makeTerminalTab(for:cwd:command:title:)` (`:1277`) |
| Self-heal against dead ids | `pruneWorkroomSplitToLiveLeaves`, `validatedSelection`, `orderedActiveTargets` |

**DRY flag:** the plan invents `TabSession` as a *second* terminal-excluding projection of `TabContent`. `NavPayload` is already that projection, and its own doc comment (`TerminalSessions.swift:126-128`) says the point of living there is "a fifth content kind is a compile error in ONE place instead of failing silently in several." Two projections reopens exactly that hole.

**TODOS cross-reference:** `TODOS.md:1011-1012` already carries *"Cross-relaunch persistence of the split — `workroomSplit` is session-only... Add a `Defaults` key + restore-on-load if wanted."* This plan absorbs that item; it should be struck in the same PR.

**Search check [Layer 1] — the built-in exists, and declining it is right, but not for the reason the plan gives.** AppKit/SwiftUI window restoration does "reopen every window that was open at quit" natively — `WindowSeed` is `Codable` precisely because value-based `WindowGroup` restoration wants it, and restored scene values come back with their **original UUIDs**, which is exactly the cross-launch window identity the plan says doesn't exist. It's suppressed by one line (`AppStore.swift:971`), added in `642d2c01` for one stated reason: *"Enforce single-window-on-launch."* You just reversed that product decision.

Measured, though: restoration is gated on the system pref. `defaults read -g NSQuitAlwaysKeepsWindows` → `1` on your machine, but the macOS default is off ("Close windows when quitting an application" ships checked). Leaning on the built-in means the feature silently does nothing for most users. **So hand-rolling is correct — the plan just justifies it as "SwiftUI's opaque restoration" when the real reason is that the built-in is user-pref-gated.** Keep `isRestorable = false` (it also stops OS-restored and app-restored windows doubling up); fix the rationale.

**Complexity check: TRIGGERS.** 9 source files (3 new) + 6 test files; 3 new behaviour-bearing units (`SessionStore`, the save coordinator, the snapshot module) plus `@Lossy`.

options.label: Split into two PRs (recommended)
options.description:
ELI10: Ship the same total scope in two landings. PR1 = panels come back in one window (schema, file store, capture, the TerminalSessions restore primitive, workroom splits, tests). PR2 = every window comes back (window identity, the ProjectStore claim gate, sibling openWindow fan-out, frame precedence, terminate freeze). PR2 is the quarter of the change with the widest blast radius — it touches window lifecycle, quit, and the shared ProjectStore — and it gets to land on a panel-restore path that has already been proven live rather than on paper.

Stakes if we pick wrong: one big landing means a window-lifecycle bug and a pane-restore bug arrive together, and bisecting "why did my layout come back wrong" spans both.

Recommendation: split — your plan already sequences them as steps 1-3/5 and step 4, so the cut costs almost nothing and halves what any single regression can be.

Completeness: 10/10 — identical total scope, just two landings.

✅ PR2's risky surface (quit path, window identity, the shared ProjectStore claim gate) lands against a panel restore you have already used for a few days, so a regression has one obvious author
✅ PR1 is independently valuable and independently revertable — if multi-window restore turns out to fight macOS, you still keep panels
❌ Two review cycles and two merges instead of one; the multi-window ask lands a few days later than it otherwise would (human: ~1 week / CC: ~3 hrs total either way)

options.label: One PR, full scope as planned
options.description:
ELI10: Build and land all six steps together — panels and multi-window restore arrive in one change.

Stakes if we pick wrong: a single 15-file diff where a window-lifecycle bug and a pane-restore bug are indistinguishable from the outside, both on the launch path.

Completeness: 10/10.

✅ One review, one merge, and the feature is whole the first time a user sees it — no half-restored state where panels return but windows don't
✅ The two halves genuinely share plumbing (the claimed session carries both the frame and the panels), so splitting does mean writing one seam twice
❌ Puts window identity, the quit path, the shared ProjectStore gate and the pane restore into one landing, all on the launch path — the one code path where a bug greets every user before they can do anything about it

options.label: Panels only — drop multi-window
options.description:
ELI10: Restore panels and layouts into the single launch window, and leave every-window restore out entirely.

Stakes if we pick wrong: you asked for every window to come back; this doesn't deliver that, and a user with two windows gets one back with the other's panels nowhere.

Completeness: 6/10 — drops a stated requirement.

✅ Smallest diff by a wide margin: no window identity, no claim gate, no sibling fan-out, no terminate freeze
✅ Zero risk to the window lifecycle and the quit path, which is where the scariest failure modes live
❌ Reverses a decision you made ten minutes ago, and the schema would carry a windows[] array with nothing ever filling slot two (human: ~3 days / CC: ~90 min)

3	## Review Sections (after scope is agreed)
4	
5	**Anti-skip rule:** Never condense, abbreviate, or skip any review section (1-4) regardless of plan type (strategy, spec, code, infra). Every section in this skill exists for a reason. "This is a strategy doc so implementation sections don't apply" is always wrong — implementation details are where strategy breaks down. If a section genuinely has zero findings, say "No issues found" and move on — but you must evaluate it.
6	
7	**Anti-shortcut clause:** The plan file is the OUTPUT of the interactive review, not a substitute for it. Writing every finding into one plan write and calling ExitPlanMode without firing AskUserQuestion is the precise failure mode of the May 2026 transcript bug — the model explored, found issues, and dumped them into a deliverable rather than walking the user through them. If you have ANY non-trivial finding in any review section, the path from finding to ExitPlanMode goes THROUGH AskUserQuestion. Zero findings in every section is the only path to ExitPlanMode that bypasses AskUserQuestion. If you find yourself wanting to write a plan with findings before asking, stop and call AskUserQuestion now — that's the bug, recognize it.
8	
9	## Prior Learnings
10	
11	Search for relevant learnings from previous sessions:
12	
13	```bash
14	_CROSS_PROJ=$(~/.claude/skills/gstack/bin/gstack-config get cross_project_learnings 2>/dev/null || echo "unset")
15	echo "CROSS_PROJECT: $_CROSS_PROJ"
16	if [ "$_CROSS_PROJ" = "true" ]; then
17	  ~/.claude/skills/gstack/bin/gstack-learnings-search --limit 10 --cross-project 2>/dev/null || true
18	else
19	  ~/.claude/skills/gstack/bin/gstack-learnings-search --limit 10 2>/dev/null || true
20	fi
21	```
22	
23	If `CROSS_PROJECT` is `unset` (first time): Use AskUserQuestion:
24	
25	> gstack can search learnings from your other projects on this machine to find
26	> patterns that might apply here. This stays local (no data leaves your machine).
27	> Recommended for solo developers. Skip if you work on multiple client codebases
28	> where cross-contamination would be a concern.
29	
30	Options:
31	- A) Enable cross-project learnings (recommended)
32	- B) Keep learnings project-scoped only
33	
34	If A: run `~/.claude/skills/gstack/bin/gstack-config set cross_project_learnings true`
35	If B: run `~/.claude/skills/gstack/bin/gstack-config set cross_project_learnings false`
36	
37	Then re-run the search with the appropriate flag.
38	
39	If learnings are found, incorporate them into your analysis. When a review finding
40	matches a past learning, display:
41	
42	**"Prior learning applied: [key] (confidence N/10, from [date])"**
43	
44	This makes the compounding visible. The user should see that gstack is getting
45	smarter on their codebase over time.
46	
47	### 1. Architecture review
48	Evaluate:
49	* Overall system design and component boundaries.
50	* Dependency graph and coupling concerns.
51	* Data flow patterns and potential bottlenecks.
52	* Scaling characteristics and single points of failure.
53	* Security architecture (auth, data access, API boundaries).
54	* Whether key flows deserve ASCII diagrams in the plan or in code comments.
55	* For each new codepath or integration point, describe one realistic production failure scenario and whether the plan accounts for it.
56	* **Distribution architecture:** If this introduces a new artifact (binary, package, container), how does it get built, published, and updated? Is the CI/CD pipeline part of the plan or deferred?
57	
58	For each issue found in this section, call AskUserQuestion individually. One issue per call. Present options, state your recommendation, explain WHY. Do NOT batch multiple issues into one AskUserQuestion. Use the preamble's AskUserQuestion Format section. The AskUserQuestion call is a tool_use, not prose — call the tool directly.
59	
60	**STOP.** Do NOT proceed to the next review section, edit the plan file with the proposed fix, or call ExitPlanMode until the user responds. An issue with an "obvious fix" is still an issue and still needs explicit user approval before it lands in the plan. Loading the AskUserQuestion schema via ToolSearch and then writing the recommendation as chat prose is the failure mode this gate exists to prevent.
61	
62	## Confidence Calibration
63	
64	Every finding MUST include a confidence score (1-10):
65	
66	| Score | Meaning | Display rule |
67	|-------|---------|-------------|
68	| 9-10 | Verified by reading specific code. Concrete bug or exploit demonstrated. | Show normally |
69	| 7-8 | High confidence pattern match. Very likely correct. | Show normally |
70	| 5-6 | Moderate. Could be a false positive. | Show with caveat: "Medium confidence, verify this is actually an issue" |
71	| 3-4 | Low confidence. Pattern is suspicious but may be fine. | Suppress from main report. Include in appendix only. |
72	| 1-2 | Speculation. | Only report if severity would be P0. |

75

82	### Pre-emit verification gate (#1539 — kills the "field doesn't exist" FP class)
83	
84	Before any finding is promoted to the report, the gate requires:
85	
86	1. **Quote the specific code line that motivates the finding** — file:line plus
87	   the verbatim text of the line(s) that triggered it. If the finding is "field
88	   X doesn't exist on model Y", quote the lines of class Y where the field
89	   would live. If "dict.get() might return None", quote the dict initialization.
90	   If "race condition between A and B", quote both A and B.
91	
92	2. **If you cannot quote the motivating line(s), the finding is unverified.**
93	   Force its confidence to 4-5 (suppressed from the main report). It still goes
94	   into the appendix so reviewers can audit calibration, but the user does NOT
95	   see it in the critical-pass output. Do not work around this by inventing
96	   speculative confidence 7+ — that defeats the gate.
97	
98	**Framework-meta nudge:** When the symbol is generated by a framework
99	metaclass, descriptor, ORM Meta inner-class, or migration history (Django
100	`Meta`, Rails `has_many`/`scope`, SQLAlchemy `relationship`/`Column`,
101	TypeORM decorators, Sequelize `init`/`belongsTo`, Prisma generated client),
102	quote the meta-construct (the `Meta` block, the migration, the decorator,
103	the schema file) instead of expecting the literal name in the class body.
104	The verification is "I read the source that creates this symbol", not "I
105	grep'd for the name and didn't find it." Deeper framework-aware verification
106	(model introspection, migration-history-aware checks, ORM dialect detection)
107	is deliberately out of scope for the lighter gate — see the deferred
108	`~/.gstack-dev/plans/1539-framework-aware-review.md` design doc.
109	
110	The FP classes the gate kills (measured against Django Sprint 2.5 #1539):
111	
112	| FP class | Why the gate catches it |
113	|---|---|
114	| "field doesn't exist on model" | Requires quoting the model class body or Meta; the field's absence becomes obvious |
115	| "dict.get() might be None" | Requires quoting the dict initialization (e.g. Django form's `cleaned_data` is `{}`-initialized) |
116	| "save() might lose fields" | Requires quoting the ORM signature or model definition |
117	| "update_fields might miss X" | Requires quoting the field set; if X doesn't exist, the FP is self-evident |
118	
119	**Calibration learning:** If you report a finding with confidence < 7 and the user
120	confirms it IS a real issue, that is a calibration event. Your initial confidence was
121	too low. Log the corrected pattern as a learning so future reviews catch it with
122	higher confidence.

163	**Step 1. Trace every codepath in the plan:**
164	
165	Read the plan document. For each new feature, service, endpoint, or component described, trace how data will flow through the code — don't just list planned functions, actually follow the planned execution:
166	
167	1. **Read the plan.** For each planned component, understand what it does and how it connects to existing code.
168	2. **Trace data flow.** Starting from each entry point (route handler, exported function, event listener, component render), follow the data through every branch:
169	   - Where does input come from? (request params, props, database, API call)
170	   - What transforms it? (validation, mapping, computation)
171	   - Where does it go? (database write, API response, rendered output, side effect)
172	   - What can go wrong at each step? (null/undefined, invalid input, network failure, empty collection)
173	3. **Diagram the execution.** For each changed file, draw an ASCII diagram showing:
174	   - Every function/method that was added or modified
175	   - Every conditional branch (if/else, switch, ternary, guard clause, early return)
176	   - Every error path (try/catch, rescue, error boundary, fallback)
177	   - Every call to another function (trace into it — does IT have untested branches?)
178	   - Every edge: what happens with null input? Empty array? Invalid type?
179	
180	This is the critical step — you're building a map of every line of code that can execute differently based on input. Every branch in this diagram needs a test.
181	
182	**Step 2. Map user flows, interactions, and error states:**
183	
184	Code coverage isn't enough — you need to cover how real users interact with the changed code. For each changed feature, think through:
185	
186	- **User flows:** What sequence of actions does a user take that touches this code? Map the full journey (e.g., "user clicks 'Pay' → form validates → API call → success/failure screen"). Each step in the journey needs a test.
187	- **Interaction edge cases:** What happens when the user does something unexpected?
188	  - Double-click/rapid resubmit
189	  - Navigate away mid-operation (back button, close tab, click another link)
190	  - Submit with stale data (page sat open for 30 minutes, session expired)
191	  - Slow connection (API takes 10 seconds — what does the user see?)
192	  - Concurrent actions (two tabs, same form)
193	- **Error states the user can see:** For every error the code handles, what does the user actually experience?
194	  - Is there a clear error message or a silent failure?
195	  - Can the user recover (retry, go back, fix input) or are they stuck?
196	  - What happens with no network? With a 500 from the API? With invalid data from the server?
197	- **Empty/zero/boundary states:** What does the UI show with zero results? With 10,000 results? With a single character input? With maximum-length input?
198	
199	Add these to your diagram alongside the code branches. A user flow with no test is just as much a gap as an untested if/else.
200	
201	**Step 3. Check each branch against existing tests:**
202	
203	Go through your diagram branch by branch — both code paths AND user flows. For each one, search for a test that exercises it:
204	- Function `processPayment()` → look for `billing.test.ts`, `billing.spec.ts`, `test/billing_test.rb`
205	- An if/else → look for tests covering BOTH the true AND false path
206	- An error handler → look for a test that triggers that specific error condition
207	- A call to `helperFn()` that has its own branches → those branches need tests too
208	- A user flow → look for an integration or E2E test that walks through the journey
209	- An interaction edge case → look for a test that simulates the unexpected action
210	
211	Quality scoring rubric:
212	- ★★★  Tests behavior with edge cases AND error paths
213	- ★★   Tests correct behavior, happy path only
214	- ★    Smoke test / existence check / trivial assertion (e.g., "it renders", "it doesn't throw")

216	### E2E Test Decision Matrix
217	
218	When checking each branch, also determine whether a unit test or E2E/integration test is the right tool:
219	
220	**RECOMMEND E2E (mark as [→E2E] in the diagram):**
221	- Common user flow spanning 3+ components/services (e.g., signup → verify email → first login)
222	- Integration point where mocking hides real failures (e.g., API → queue → worker → DB)
223	- Auth/payment/data-destruction flows — too important to trust unit tests alone
224	
225	**RECOMMEND EVAL (mark as [→EVAL] in the diagram):**
226	- Critical LLM call that needs a quality eval (e.g., prompt change → test output still meets quality bar)
227	- Changes to prompt templates, system instructions, or tool definitions
228	
229	**STICK WITH UNIT TESTS:**
230	- Pure function with clear inputs/outputs
231	- Internal helper with no side effects
232	- Edge case of a single function (null input, empty array)
233	- Obscure/rare flow that isn't customer-facing

235	### REGRESSION RULE (mandatory)
236	
237	**IRON RULE:** When the coverage audit identifies a REGRESSION — code that previously worked but the diff broke — a regression test is added to the plan as a critical requirement. No AskUserQuestion. No skipping. Regressions are the highest-priority test because they prove something broke.
238	
239	A regression is when:
240	- The diff modifies existing behavior (not new code)
241	- The existing test suite (if any) doesn't cover the changed path
242	- The change introduces a new failure mode for existing callers
243	
244	When uncertain whether a change is a regression, err on the side of writing the test.

## Review Sections (after scope is agreed)

**Anti-skip rule:** Never condense, abbreviate, or skip any review section (1-4) regardless of plan type (strategy, spec, code, infra). Every section in this skill exists for a reason. "This is a strategy doc so implementation sections don't apply" is always wrong — implementation details are where strategy breaks down. If a section genuinely has zero findings, say "No issues found" and move on — but you must evaluate it.

**Anti-shortcut clause:** The plan file is the OUTPUT of the interactive review, not a substitute for it. Writing every finding into one plan write and calling ExitPlanMode without firing AskUserQuestion is the precise failure mode of the May 2026 transcript bug — the model explored, found issues, and dumped them into a deliverable rather than walking the user through them. If you have ANY non-trivial finding in any review section, the path from finding to ExitPlanMode goes THROUGH AskUserQuestion. Zero findings in every section is the only path to ExitPlanMode that bypasses AskUserQuestion. If you find yourself wanting to write a plan with findings before asking, stop and call AskUserQuestion now — that's the bug, recognize it.

## Prior Learnings

Search for relevant learnings from previous sessions:

```bash
_CROSS_PROJ=$(~/.claude/skills/gstack/bin/gstack-config get cross_project_learnings 2>/dev/null || echo "unset")
echo "CROSS_PROJECT: $_CROSS_PROJ"
if [ "$_CROSS_PROJ" = "true" ]; then
  ~/.claude/skills/gstack/bin/gstack-learnings-search --limit 10 --cross-project 2>/dev/null || true
else
  ~/.claude/skills/gstack/bin/gstack-learnings-search --limit 10 2>/dev/null || true
fi
```

If `CROSS_PROJECT` is `unset` (first time): Use AskUserQuestion:

> gstack can search learnings from your other projects on this machine to find
> patterns that might apply here. This stays local (no data leaves your machine).
> Recommended for solo developers. Skip if you work on multiple client codebases
> where cross-contamination would be a concern.

Options:
- A) Enable cross-project learnings (recommended)
- B) Keep learnings project-scoped only

If A: run `~/.claude/skills/gstack/bin/gstack-config set cross_project_learnings true`
If B: run `~/.claude/skills/gstack/bin/gstack-config set cross_project_learnings false`

Then re-run the search with the appropriate flag.

If learnings are found, incorporate them into your analysis. When a review finding
matches a past learning, display:

**"Prior learning applied: [key] (confidence N/10, from [date])"**

This makes the compounding visible. The user should see that gstack is getting
smarter on their codebase over time.

### 1. Architecture review
Evaluate:
* Overall system design and component boundaries.
* Dependency graph and coupling concerns.
* Data flow patterns and potential bottlenecks.
* Scaling characteristics and single points of failure.
* Security architecture (auth, data access, API boundaries).
* Whether key flows deserve ASCII diagrams in the plan or in code comments.
* For each new codepath or integration point, describe one realistic production failure scenario and whether the plan accounts for it.
* **Distribution architecture:** If this introduces a new artifact (binary, package, container), how does it get built, published, and updated? Is the CI/CD pipeline part of the plan or deferred?

For each issue found in this section, call AskUserQuestion individually. One issue per call. Present options, state your recommendation, explain WHY. Do NOT batch multiple issues into one AskUserQuestion. Use the preamble's AskUserQuestion Format section. The AskUserQuestion call is a tool_use, not prose — call the tool directly.

**STOP.** Do NOT proceed to the next review section, edit the plan file with the proposed fix, or call ExitPlanMode until the user responds. An issue with an "obvious fix" is still an issue and still needs explicit user approval before it lands in the plan. Loading the AskUserQuestion schema via ToolSearch and then writing the recommendation as chat prose is the failure mode this gate exists to prevent.

## Confidence Calibration

Every finding MUST include a confidence score (1-10):

| Score | Meaning | Display rule |
|-------|---------|-------------|
| 9-10 | Verified by reading specific code. Concrete bug or exploit demonstrated. | Show normally |
| 7-8 | High confidence pattern match. Very likely correct. | Show normally |
| 5-6 | Moderate. Could be a false positive. | Show with caveat: "Medium confidence, verify this is actually an issue" |
| 3-4 | Low confidence. Pattern is suspicious but may be fine. | Suppress from main report. Include in appendix only. |
| 1-2 | Speculation. | Only report if severity would be P0. |

**Finding format:**

\`[SEVERITY] (confidence: N/10) file:line — description\`

Example:
\`[P1] (confidence: 9/10) app/models/user.rb:42 — SQL injection via string interpolation in where clause\`
\`[P2] (confidence: 5/10) app/controllers/api/v1/users_controller.rb:18 — Possible N+1 query, verify with production logs\`

### Pre-emit verification gate (#1539 — kills the "field doesn't exist" FP class)

Before any finding is promoted to the report, the gate requires:

1. **Quote the specific code line that motivates the finding** — file:line plus
   the verbatim text of the line(s) that triggered it. If the finding is "field
   X doesn't exist on model Y", quote the lines of class Y where the field
   would live. If "dict.get() might return None", quote the dict initialization.
   If "race condition between A and B", quote both A and B.

2. **If you cannot quote the motivating line(s), the finding is unverified.**
   Force its confidence to 4-5 (suppressed from the main report). It still goes
   into the appendix so reviewers can audit calibration, but the user does NOT
   see it in the critical-pass output. Do not work around this by inventing
   speculative confidence 7+ — that defeats the gate.

**Framework-meta nudge:** When the symbol is generated by a framework
metaclass, descriptor, ORM Meta inner-class, or migration history (Django
`Meta`, Rails `has_many`/`scope`, SQLAlchemy `relationship`/`Column`,
TypeORM decorators, Sequelize `init`/`belongsTo`, Prisma generated client),
quote the meta-construct (the `Meta` block, the migration, the decorator,
the schema file) instead of expecting the literal name in the class body.
The verification is "I read the source that creates this symbol", not "I
grep'd for the name and didn't find it." Deeper framework-aware verification
(model introspection, migration-history-aware checks, ORM dialect detection)
is deliberately out of scope for the lighter gate — see the deferred
`~/.gstack-dev/plans/1539-framework-aware-review.md` design doc.

The FP classes the gate kills (measured against Django Sprint 2.5 #1539):

| FP class | Why the gate catches it |
|---|---|
| "field doesn't exist on model" | Requires quoting the model class body or Meta; the field's absence becomes obvious |
| "dict.get() might be None" | Requires quoting the dict initialization (e.g. Django form's `cleaned_data` is `{}`-initialized) |
| "save() might lose fields" | Requires quoting the ORM signature or model definition |
| "update_fields might miss X" | Requires quoting the field set; if X doesn't exist, the FP is self-evident |

**Calibration learning:** If you report a finding with confidence < 7 and the user
confirms it IS a real issue, that is a calibration event. Your initial confidence was
too low. Log the corrected pattern as a learning so future reviews catch it with
higher confidence.

### 2. Code quality review
Evaluate:
* Code organization and module structure.
* DRY violations—be aggressive here.
* Error handling patterns and missing edge cases (call these out explicitly).
* Technical debt hotspots.
* Areas that are over-engineered or under-engineered relative to my preferences.
* Existing ASCII diagrams in touched files — are they still accurate after this change?

For each issue found in this section, call AskUserQuestion individually. One issue per call. Present options, state your recommendation, explain WHY. Do NOT batch multiple issues into one AskUserQuestion. Use the preamble's AskUserQuestion Format section. The AskUserQuestion call is a tool_use, not prose — call the tool directly.

**STOP.** Do NOT proceed to the next review section, edit the plan file with the proposed fix, or call ExitPlanMode until the user responds. An issue with an "obvious fix" is still an issue and still needs explicit user approval before it lands in the plan. Loading the AskUserQuestion schema via ToolSearch and then writing the recommendation as chat prose is the failure mode this gate exists to prevent.

### 3. Test review

100% coverage is the goal. Evaluate every codepath in the plan and ensure the plan includes tests for each one. If the plan is missing tests, add them — the plan should be complete enough that implementation includes full test coverage from the start.

### Test Framework Detection

Before analyzing coverage, detect the project's test framework:

1. **Read CLAUDE.md** — look for a `## Testing` section with test command and framework name. If found, use that as the authoritative source.
2. **If CLAUDE.md has no testing section, auto-detect:**

```bash
setopt +o nomatch 2>/dev/null || true  # zsh compat
# Detect project runtime
[ -f Gemfile ] && echo "RUNTIME:ruby"
[ -f package.json ] && echo "RUNTIME:node"
[ -f requirements.txt ] || [ -f pyproject.toml ] && echo "RUNTIME:python"
[ -f go.mod ] && echo "RUNTIME:go"
[ -f Cargo.toml ] && echo "RUNTIME:rust"
# Check for existing test infrastructure
ls jest.config.* vitest.config.* playwright.config.* cypress.config.* .rspec pytest.ini phpunit.xml 2>/dev/null
ls -d test/ tests/ spec/ __tests__/ cypress/ e2e/ 2>/dev/null
```

3. **If no framework detected:** still produce the coverage diagram, but skip test generation.

**Step 1. Trace every codepath in the plan:**

Read the plan document. For each new feature, service, endpoint, or component described, trace how data will flow through the code — don't just list planned functions, actually follow the planned execution:

1. **Read the plan.** For each planned component, understand what it does and how it connects to existing code.
2. **Trace data flow.** Starting from each entry point (route handler, exported function, event listener, component render), follow the data through every branch:
   - Where does input come from? (request params, props, database, API call)
   - What transforms it? (validation, mapping, computation)
   - Where does it go? (database write, API response, rendered output, side effect)
   - What can go wrong at each step? (null/undefined, invalid input, network failure, empty collection)
3. **Diagram the execution.** For each changed file, draw an ASCII diagram showing:
   - Every function/method that was added or modified
   - Every conditional branch (if/else, switch, ternary, guard clause, early return)
   - Every error path (try/catch, rescue, error boundary, fallback)
   - Every call to another function (trace into it — does IT have untested branches?)
   - Every edge: what happens with null input? Empty array? Invalid type?

This is the critical step — you're building a map of every line of code that can execute differently based on input. Every branch in this diagram needs a test.

**Step 2. Map user flows, interactions, and error states:**

Code coverage isn't enough — you need to cover how real users interact with the changed code. For each changed feature, think through:

- **User flows:** What sequence of actions does a user take that touches this code? Map the full journey (e.g., "user clicks 'Pay' → form validates → API call → success/failure screen"). Each step in the journey needs a test.
- **Interaction edge cases:** What happens when the user does something unexpected?
  - Double-click/rapid resubmit
  - Navigate away mid-operation (back button, close tab, click another link)
  - Submit with stale data (page sat open for 30 minutes, session expired)
  - Slow connection (API takes 10 seconds — what does the user see?)
  - Concurrent actions (two tabs, same form)
- **Error states the user can see:** For every error the code handles, what does the user actually experience?
  - Is there a clear error message or a silent failure?
  - Can the user recover (retry, go back, fix input) or are they stuck?
  - What happens with no network? With a 500 from the API? With invalid data from the server?
- **Empty/zero/boundary states:** What does the UI show with zero results? With 10,000 results? With a single character input? With maximum-length input?

Add these to your diagram alongside the code branches. A user flow with no test is just as much a gap as an untested if/else.

**Step 3. Check each branch against existing tests:**

Go through your diagram branch by branch — both code paths AND user flows. For each one, search for a test that exercises it:
- Function `processPayment()` → look for `billing.test.ts`, `billing.spec.ts`, `test/billing_test.rb`
- An if/else → look for tests covering BOTH the true AND false path
- An error handler → look for a test that triggers that specific error condition
- A call to `helperFn()` that has its own branches → those branches need tests too
- A user flow → look for an integration or E2E test that walks through the journey
- An interaction edge case → look for a test that simulates the unexpected action

Quality scoring rubric:
- ★★★  Tests behavior with edge cases AND error paths
- ★★   Tests correct behavior, happy path only
- ★    Smoke test / existence check / trivial assertion (e.g., "it renders", "it doesn't throw")

### E2E Test Decision Matrix

When checking each branch, also determine whether a unit test or E2E/integration test is the right tool:

**RECOMMEND E2E (mark as [→E2E] in the diagram):**
- Common user flow spanning 3+ components/services (e.g., signup → verify email → first login)
- Integration point where mocking hides real failures (e.g., API → queue → worker → DB)
- Auth/payment/data-destruction flows — too important to trust unit tests alone

**RECOMMEND EVAL (mark as [→EVAL] in the diagram):**
- Critical LLM call that needs a quality eval (e.g., prompt change → test output still meets quality bar)
- Changes to prompt templates, system instructions, or tool definitions

**STICK WITH UNIT TESTS:**
- Pure function with clear inputs/outputs
- Internal helper with no side effects
- Edge case of a single function (null input, empty array)
- Obscure/rare flow that isn't customer-facing

### REGRESSION RULE (mandatory)

**IRON RULE:** When the coverage audit identifies a REGRESSION — code that previously worked but the diff broke — a regression test is added to the plan as a critical requirement. No AskUserQuestion. No skipping. Regressions are the highest-priority test because they prove something broke.

A regression is when:
- The diff modifies existing behavior (not new code)
- The existing test suite (if any) doesn't cover the changed path
- The change introduces a new failure mode for existing callers

When uncertain whether a change is a regression, err on the side of writing the test.

**Step 4. Output ASCII coverage diagram:**

Include BOTH code paths and user flows in the same diagram. Mark E2E-worthy and eval-worthy paths:

```
CODE PATHS                                            USER FLOWS
[+] src/services/billing.ts                           [+] Payment checkout
  ├── processPayment()                                  ├── [★★★ TESTED] Complete purchase — checkout.e2e.ts:15
  │   ├── [★★★ TESTED] happy + declined + timeout      ├── [GAP] [→E2E] Double-click submit
  │   ├── [GAP]         Network timeout                 └── [GAP]        Navigate away mid-payment
  │   └── [GAP]         Invalid currency
  └── refundPayment()                                 [+] Error states
      ├── [★★  TESTED] Full refund — :89                ├── [★★  TESTED] Card declined message
      └── [★   TESTED] Partial (non-throw only) — :101  └── [GAP]        Network timeout UX

LLM integration: [GAP] [→EVAL] Prompt template change — needs eval test

COVERAGE: 5/13 paths tested (38%)  |  Code paths: 3/5 (60%)  |  User flows: 2/8 (25%)
QUALITY: ★★★:2 ★★:2 ★:1  |  GAPS: 8 (2 E2E, 1 eval)
```

Legend: ★★★ behavior + edge + error  |  ★★ happy path  |  ★ smoke check
[→E2E] = needs integration test  |  [→EVAL] = needs LLM eval

**Fast path:** All paths covered → "Test review: All new code paths have test coverage ✓" Continue.

**Step 5. Add missing tests to the plan:**

For each GAP identified in the diagram, add a test requirement to the plan. Be specific:
- What test file to create (match existing naming conventions)
- What the test should assert (specific inputs → expected outputs/behavior)
- Whether it's a unit test, E2E test, or eval (use the decision matrix)
- For regressions: flag as **CRITICAL** and explain what broke

The plan should be complete enough that when implementation begins, every test is written alongside the feature code — not deferred to a follow-up.

### Test Plan Artifact

After producing the coverage diagram, write a test plan artifact to the project directory so `/qa` and `/qa-only` can consume it as primary test input:

```bash
eval "$(~/.claude/skills/gstack/bin/gstack-slug 2>/dev/null)" && mkdir -p ~/.gstack/projects/$SLUG
USER=$(whoami)
DATETIME=$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)
```

Write to `~/.gstack/projects/{slug}/{user}-{branch}-eng-review-test-plan-{datetime}.md`:

```markdown
# Test Plan
Generated by /plan-eng-review on {date}
Branch: {branch}
Repo: {owner/repo}

## Affected Pages/Routes
- {URL path} — {what to test and why}

## Key Interactions to Verify
- {interaction description} on {page}

## Edge Cases
- {edge case} on {page}

## Critical Paths
- {end-to-end flow that must work}
```

This file is consumed by `/qa` and `/qa-only` as primary test input. Include only the information that helps a QA tester know **what to test and where** — not implementation details.

For LLM/prompt changes: check the "Prompt/LLM changes" file patterns listed in CLAUDE.md. If this plan touches ANY of those patterns, state which eval suites must be run, which cases should be added, and what baselines to compare against. Then use AskUserQuestion to confirm the eval scope with the user.

For each issue found in this section, call AskUserQuestion individually. One issue per call. Present options, state your recommendation, explain WHY. Do NOT batch multiple issues into one AskUserQuestion. Use the preamble's AskUserQuestion Format section. The AskUserQuestion call is a tool_use, not prose — call the tool directly.

Loading the AskUserQuestion schema via ToolSearch and then writing the recommendation as chat prose is the failure mode this gate exists to prevent.

### 4. Performance review
Evaluate:
* N+1 queries and database access patterns.
* Memory-usage concerns.
* Caching opportunities.
* Slow or high-complexity code paths.

Loading the AskUserQuestion schema via ToolSearch and then writing the recommendation as chat prose is the failure mode this gate exists to prevent.

## Outside Voice — Independent Plan Challenge (default-on)

After all review sections are complete, run an independent second opinion from a
different AI system automatically — it is a standard part of plan review, not an
opt-in. Two models agreeing on a plan is stronger signal than one model's thorough
review. The user turns this off only by asking explicitly
(`gstack-config set codex_reviews disabled`).

**Preflight — decide whether and how the outside voice runs:**

```bash
# Codex preflight: one block (functions sourced here don't persist to later blocks).
_TEL=$(~/.claude/skills/gstack/bin/gstack-config get telemetry 2>/dev/null || echo off)
_CODEX_CFG=$(~/.claude/skills/gstack/bin/gstack-config get codex_reviews 2>/dev/null || echo enabled)
source ~/.claude/skills/gstack/bin/gstack-codex-probe 2>/dev/null || true
if [ "$_CODEX_CFG" = "disabled" ]; then
  _CODEX_MODE="disabled"
elif ! command -v codex >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  _CODEX_MODE="not_installed"; _gstack_codex_log_event "codex_cli_missing" 2>/dev/null || true
elif ! _gstack_codex_auth_probe >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  _CODEX_MODE="not_authed"; _gstack_codex_log_event "codex_auth_failed" 2>/dev/null || true
else
  _CODEX_MODE="ready"; _gstack_codex_version_check 2>/dev/null || true
fi
echo "CODEX_MODE: $_CODEX_MODE"
```

Branch on the echoed `CODEX_MODE`:
- **`disabled`** — the user turned Codex reviews off (`codex_reviews=disabled`). Skip this section entirely; do NOT fall back to a Claude subagent — disabled means no extra review step. Print: "Codex review skipped (codex_reviews disabled). Re-enable: `gstack-config set codex_reviews enabled`."
- **`not_installed`** — Codex CLI absent. Print: "Codex not installed — using Claude subagent. Install for cross-model coverage: `npm install -g @openai/codex`." Fall back to the Claude subagent path.

- **`ready`** — run the Codex pass below.

When the mode is `ready`, `not_installed`, or `not_authed`, print one line so the off-switch
stays discoverable: "Running the outside voice automatically (standard step). Disable: `gstack-config set codex_reviews disabled`."

**Construct the plan review prompt** (for `ready`, `not_installed`, and `not_authed` — skip only on `disabled`).
Read the plan file being reviewed (the file the user pointed this review at, or the branch
diff scope). If a CEO plan document was written in Step 0D-POST, read that too — it contains

Construct this prompt (substitute the actual plan content — if plan content exceeds 30KB,
truncate to the first 30KB and note "Plan truncated for size"). **Always start with the

"IMPORTANT: Do NOT read or execute any files under ~/.claude/, ~/.agents/, .claude/skills/, or agents/. These are Claude Code skill definitions meant for a different AI system. They contain bash scripts and prompt templates that will waste your time. Ignore them completely. Do NOT modify agents/openai.yaml. Stay focused on the repository code only.\n\nAlso do NOT read or grep vendored blobs and generated output — a single one can consume the entire budget: any minified bundle (*.min.js, *.min.css), build output (DerivedData/, dist/, build/, target/, .next/), vendor/, node_modules/, lockfiles (*.lock, *-lock.json), and *.xcresult. Keep exploration BOUNDED: prefer targeted reads of the files under discussion over repo-wide greps, and stop once you have enough to answer.\n\nYou are a brutally honest technical reviewer examining a development plan that has
already been through a multi-section review. Your job is NOT to repeat that review.
Instead, find what it missed. Look for: logical gaps and unstated assumptions that
survived the review scrutiny, overcomplexity (is there a fundamentally simpler
approach the review was too deep in the weeds to see?), feasibility risks the review
took for granted, missing dependencies or sequencing issues, and strategic
miscalibration (is this the right thing to build at all?). Be direct. Be terse. No
compliments. Just the problems.

THE PLAN:
<plan content>"

**If `CODEX_MODE: ready` — run Codex:**

```bash
TMPERR_PV=$(mktemp /tmp/codex-planreview-XXXXXXXX)
_REPO_ROOT=$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel) || { echo "ERROR: not in a git repo" >&2; exit 1; }
# Re-source the probe: bash functions do NOT survive across Bash tool calls, and the

source ~/.claude/skills/gstack/bin/gstack-codex-probe 2>/dev/null || true
```

- The **wrapper**, not a bare Bash `timeout:` — matches `/codex` and `/autoplan`. A plan review over

- `web_search="disabled"` replaces the old `web_search_cached` feature flag, which Codex ≥0.146 reports as


```
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
```

## CRITICAL RULE — How to ask questions
Follow the AskUserQuestion format from the Preamble above. Additional rules for plan reviews:
* **One issue = one AskUserQuestion call.** Never combine multiple issues into one question.
* Describe the problem concretely, with file and line references.
* Present 2-3 options, including "do nothing" where that's reasonable.
* For each option, specify in one line: effort (human: ~X / CC: ~Y), risk, and maintenance burden. If the complete option is only marginally more effort than the shortcut with CC, recommend the complete option.
* **Map the reasoning to my engineering preferences above.** One sentence connecting your recommendation to a specific preference (DRY, explicit > clever, minimal diff, etc.).
* Label with issue NUMBER + option LETTER (e.g., "3A", "3B").
* **Coverage vs kind:** for every per-issue AskUserQuestion you raise in this review, decide whether the options differ in coverage or in kind. If coverage (e.g., more tests vs fewer, complete error handling vs happy-path-only, full edge-case coverage vs shortcut), include `Completeness: N/10` on each option. If kind (e.g., architectural choice between two different systems, posture-over-posture, A/B/C where each is a different kind of thing), skip the score and add one line: `Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.` Do NOT fabricate scores on kind-differentiated questions — filler scores are worse than no score.
* **Zero findings:** if a section has zero findings, state "No issues, moving on" and proceed. Otherwise, use AskUserQuestion for each finding — a finding with an "obvious fix" is still a finding and still needs user approval before any change lands in the plan.

## Required outputs

### "NOT in scope" section
Every plan review MUST produce a "NOT in scope" section listing work that was considered and explicitly deferred, with a one-line rationale for each item.

### "What already exists" section
List existing code/flows that already partially solve sub-problems in this plan, and whether the plan reuses them or unnecessarily rebuilds them.

### TODOS.md updates
After all review sections are complete, present each potential TODO as its own individual AskUserQuestion. Never batch TODOs — one per question. Never silently skip this step. Follow the format in `.claude/skills/review/TODOS-format.md`.

For each TODO, describe:
* **What:** One-line description of the work.
* **Why:** The concrete problem it solves or value it unlocks.
* **Pros:** What you gain by doing this work.
* **Cons:** Cost, complexity, or risks of doing it.
* **Context:** Enough detail that someone picking this up in 3 months understands the motivation, the current state, and where to start.
* **Depends on / blocked by:** Any prerequisites or ordering constraints.

Then present options: **A)** Add to TODOS.md **B)** Skip — not valuable enough **C)** Build it now in this PR instead of deferring.

Do NOT just append vague bullet points. A TODO without context is worse than no TODO — it creates false confidence that the idea was captured while actually losing the reasoning.

### Diagrams
The plan itself should use ASCII diagrams for any non-trivial data flow, state machine, or processing pipeline. Additionally, identify which files in the implementation should get inline ASCII diagram comments — particularly Models with complex state transitions, Services with multi-step pipelines, and Concerns with non-obvious mixin behavior.

### Failure modes
For each new codepath identified in the test review diagram, list one realistic way it could fail in production (timeout, nil reference, race condition, stale data, etc.) and whether:
1. A test covers that failure
2. Error handling exists for it
3. The user would see a clear error or a silent failure

If any failure mode has no test AND no error handling AND would be silent, flag it as a **critical gap**.

### Worktree parallelization strategy

Analyze the plan's implementation steps for parallel execution opportunities. This helps the user split work across git worktrees (via Claude Code's Agent tool with `isolation: "worktree"` or parallel workspaces).

**Skip if:** all steps touch the same primary module, or the plan has fewer than 2 independent workstreams. In that case, write: "Sequential implementation, no parallelization opportunity."

**Otherwise, produce:**

1. **Dependency table** — for each implementation step/workstream:

| Step | Modules touched | Depends on |
|------|----------------|------------|
| (step name) | (directories/modules, NOT specific files) | (other steps, or —) |

Work at the module/directory level, not file level. Plans describe intent ("add API endpoints"), not specific files. Module-level ("controllers/, models/") is reliable; file-level is guesswork.

2. **Parallel lanes** — group steps into lanes:
   - Steps with no shared modules and no dependency go in separate lanes (parallel)
   - Steps sharing a module directory go in the same lane (sequential)
   - Steps depending on other steps go in later lanes

Format: `Lane A: step1 → step2 (sequential, shared models/)` / `Lane B: step3 (independent)`

3. **Execution order** — which lanes launch in parallel, which wait. Example: "Launch A + B in parallel worktrees. Merge both. Then C."

4. **Conflict flags** — if two parallel lanes touch the same module directory, flag it: "Lanes X and Y both touch module/ — potential merge conflict. Consider sequential execution or careful coordination."

questions.question: Issue 1 — the save debounce can starve. How should the write trigger guarantee forward progress? <gstack-qid:plan-eng-review-arch-debounce-starvation>

options.label: 1A) Add a max-delay ceiling (recommended)
options.description:
ELI10: Keep the coalescing debounce, but also remember when the layout first went dirty. If more than a few seconds have passed since that first dirty mark, write now regardless of how much chatter is still arriving. Standard debounce-with-max-wait. The terminal can stream output forever and the layout still gets saved every N seconds.

Stakes if we pick wrong: split a pane while a dev server is streaming, quit via crash or force-quit, and the split is gone — the exact scenario the feature exists to prevent.

Recommendation: 1A — it keeps the "a thirteenth mutation site cannot be forgotten" property that made objectWillChange the right hook, and adds a hard guarantee of forward progress. Matches your explicit-over-clever preference: the ceiling is one stored Date and one comparison, not a cleverness.

Completeness: 1A=10/10, 1B=8/10, 1C=4/10.

✅ Bounded worst-case data loss under every load, including a terminal that never goes quiet — which is the normal state of this app
✅ Costs one Date field and one branch on top of the debounce already in the plan; no new concept for a reader to learn
❌ Under sustained chatter it writes on a fixed cadence even when only the ignored fields changed, so you pay a snapshot build + hash you'd otherwise have skipped (human: ~20 min / CC: ~3 min)

options.label: 1B) Trigger only on structural mutations
options.description:
ELI10: Drop the objectWillChange sink. Instead have TerminalSessions call an onLayoutChanged closure from the ~12 places that actually change structure — add tab, close tab, split, move, focus, ratio — so title and activity noise never reaches the save path at all.

Stakes if we pick wrong: someone adds a thirteenth structural mutation in six months, forgets the callback, and that mutation silently stops being persisted — a bug with no crash and no test failure.

Completeness: 1B=8/10.

✅ No wasted work at all: the save path only ever wakes for changes that can alter the snapshot, so the digest guard becomes belt-and-braces rather than load-bearing
✅ Makes the save trigger readable — you can grep the callback and see exactly what is considered a layout change
❌ Reintroduces the forget-a-site failure mode that the plan explicitly chose objectWillChange to avoid, and it fails silently (human: ~1h / CC: ~10 min)

options.label: 1C) Keep as planned, rely on quit flush
options.description:
ELI10: Leave the cancel-and-replace debounce. Accept that during sustained terminal output nothing is written, and count on the quit and resign-active flushes to catch up.

Stakes if we pick wrong: any exit that isn't a clean quit — crash, force-quit, the libghostty EXC_BAD_ACCESS the codebase already documents — loses everything since the terminal last went quiet, which could be the whole session.

content.text:
**Issue 2 — `[P1] (confidence: 9/10)` a cancelled quit would freeze session writes for the rest of the app's life.**

The plan puts the flush *and* the freeze in `applicationShouldTerminate`, above the fixture early-return. But that method can return without terminating:

```swift
// WorkroomApp.swift:565
guard shouldQuit else { return .terminateCancel }
```

Press ⌘Q, hit Cancel in the confirm dialog, keep working — with the freeze already set, every later save is dropped and the session file is stale from that moment on. Note the existing code sets its own terminating flag *after* the cancel gate, in `stopRunCommandsThenTerminate`:

```swift
// WorkroomApp.swift:580 — reached only past the cancel guard
registry.isTerminating = true
```

questions.question: Issue 2 — where should the quit-time flush and the write-freeze actually go? <gstack-qid:plan-eng-review-arch-terminate-freeze>

options.label: 2A) Freeze beside isTerminating (recommended)
options.description:
ELI10: Put both the flush and the freeze inside stopRunCommandsThenTerminate, on the line next to registry.isTerminating = true. That code only runs once the user has actually confirmed the quit, so a cancelled quit never freezes anything. It is also still before any window closes, which is the property the freeze exists to protect.

Stakes if we pick wrong: cancel a quit once and your session silently stops being saved until you relaunch — a bug that only shows up as "my layout is from an hour ago", with nothing to point at.

Recommendation: 2A — the codebase already put its terminating flag exactly there for exactly this reason, so the session freeze inherits a correctness argument that has already been thought through.

Completeness: 2A=10/10, 2B=7/10, 2C=9/10.

✅ A cancelled quit is a no-op: nothing flushed, nothing frozen, work continues normally
✅ Sits with isTerminating so a reader sees one terminating-state concept, not two that must be kept in sync
❌ The fixture early-return at :549 short-circuits above it, so XCUITest determinism needs the flush duplicated in that branch or the fixture path handled explicitly (human: ~30 min / CC: ~5 min)

options.label: 2B) Flush early, freeze late
options.description:
ELI10: Flush at the top of applicationShouldTerminate as the plan says, but only set the freeze flag later, once the quit is confirmed. Splits the two operations that the plan treats as one.

Stakes if we pick wrong: a cancelled quit writes a snapshot that is correct but premature — harmless — while the freeze correctly stays off.

Completeness: 2B=7/10.

✅ Guarantees a write happens before the confirm dialog blocks the main thread, so a user who force-quits during the dialog still has a fresh file
✅ Cancelled quit remains fully functional; only a redundant write is spent
❌ Two flags in two places for one concept, and it leaves a window between the flush and the freeze where a close could still mutate the live window set

options.label: 2C) Freeze on a real terminating signal only
options.description:
ELI10: Don't add a new freeze flag at all — have every save check the existing WindowRegistry.isTerminating and drop the write when it's true. One flag, already set at exactly the right moment, already tested by the close-guard path.

Stakes if we pick wrong: isTerminating gains a second responsibility, so a future change to its lifecycle silently changes session behaviour too.

Completeness: 2C=9/10.

✅ Zero new state: reuses a flag that is already set at precisely the moment windows start closing, which is the exact condition the freeze cares about
✅ Fewer moving parts to test — no risk of the two flags disagreeing
❌ Overloads a flag whose documented job is "suppress the per-window close prompt during a quit"; the SIGTERM path never sets it today, so that path would need it set too

questions.question: Issue 3 — the plan adds a second TabContent projection beside NavPayload. Reuse, co-locate, or leave split? <gstack-qid:plan-eng-review-arch-dry-projection>

options.label: 3B) Separate DTO, co-located (recommended)
options.description:

Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.

questions.question: Issue 4 — window frames will live in both Defaults[.mainWindowFrame] and the session file. Which owns them? <gstack-qid:plan-eng-review-arch-frame-authority>

options.label: 4A) Session file owns frames; Defaults key is the cold-start fallback (recommended)
options.description:
ELI10: The session file becomes the authority on per-window frames, since it is the only store that can hold more than one. Keep Defaults[.mainWindowFrame] but demote it to what it can actually do correctly: the frame for a very first launch with no session file. Stop the per-window observers writing it once a session exists, so three windows no longer race one key.

Stakes if we pick wrong: two stores write the same value on every resize and disagree on restore — windows come back at the wrong size, or all at the same size, and it is nondeterministic which.

Recommendation: 4A — one value, one home, and the fallback still covers the fresh-install case the Defaults key was written for. Directly matches your explicit-over-clever preference; the alternative is two writers with an implicit precedence rule.

Completeness: 4A=10/10, 4B=6/10, 4C=8/10.

✅ Fixes the pre-existing multi-window clobber as a side effect — today three windows already fight over that one key
✅ Restore reads frames from the same place it reads panels, so a window's geometry and its contents can never come from two different sessions
❌ Touches attachWindow's observer wiring, which is load-bearing pre-display code, so it needs a careful eye on the no-flash ordering that commit 642d2c01 fought for (human: ~45 min / CC: ~8 min)

options.label: 4B) Leave both, session frame wins on restore
options.description:
ELI10: Change nothing about the existing observers. The session file also records frames, and on restore the session's frame takes precedence. Both keep writing.

Stakes if we pick wrong: the Defaults key keeps being clobbered by whichever window moved last, and it is still consulted in the fallback chain — so the wrong size can surface in the paths where the session has no entry.

Completeness: 4B=6/10.

✅ Smallest possible diff — nothing in attachWindow's delicate pre-display path changes
✅ Precedence is easy to state and easy to test in one unit test
❌ Leaves a known-wrong writer in place and adds a second one on top, so the next person debugging window sizing has two stores to reason about

options.label: 4C) Gate the existing observer to the active window
options.description:
ELI10: Fix only the existing wart: make the frame observer write Defaults[.mainWindowFrame] just for the last-active window, matching how persistsSidebarPrefs already arbitrates the other shared prefs. The session file also stores frames, but the Defaults key stops being a free-for-all.

Stakes if we pick wrong: still two writers, just better-behaved ones.

Completeness: 4C=8/10.

✅ Reuses an arbitration concept the codebase already has, so no new pattern is introduced anywhere
✅ Fixes the multi-window clobber with a one-line guard rather than a rewiring
❌ Does not resolve the two-homes problem — both stores still hold a frame, and restore still needs a precedence rule to break ties

content.text:
## Section 2 — Code quality review

**Issue 5 — `[P2] (confidence: 8/10)` `@Lossy`'s headline justification is self-defeating under the plan's own versioning rules.**

The plan sells per-element lossy decoding with: *"a newer build wrote a fifth tab kind"* → one tab missing instead of the whole session gone. And the degradation table says `Unknown TabSession.kind` → *"One tab dropped at materialise."*

But it also says `schemaVersion` newer than current → *"Ignore, restore nothing"*, and forward-compat is scoped to *"new fields are always optional."* A fifth tab **kind** is a new enum value, not a new optional field. If adding one bumps `schemaVersion`, the whole file is discarded before `@Lossy` ever runs — the lossy path is dead code for its own stated use case. `@Lossy` only pays if the versioning rule explicitly permits additive kinds at the same version.

Same trap the app already navigated once: `inspector.layout.v2` (`DefaultsKeys.swift:175`) versions the *key* to discard, while `reconcileInspectorState` (`AppStore.swift:4209`) reconciles shape — two different answers for two different change classes, deliberately.

questions.question: Issue 5 — what change classes bump schemaVersion, and does @Lossy earn its keep? <gstack-qid:plan-eng-review-cq-versioning-rule>

options.label: 5A) Additive changes never bump the version; keep @Lossy (recommended)
options.description:
ELI10: Write the rule down explicitly in the schema file header: adding a tab kind, or adding an optional field, does NOT bump schemaVersion — only a breaking reshape does. That is precisely what makes lossy decoding pay: a Nightly build writes a fifth kind, you roll back to stable, and stable drops that one tab while restoring everything else. Without the rule stated, the first person to add a kind bumps the version out of caution and silently deletes everyone's session.

Stakes if we pick wrong: a future release quietly wipes every user's saved layout on first launch, and it looks like a bug in restore rather than a versioning decision made months earlier.

Recommendation: 5A — it makes the ~20 lines of @Lossy load-bearing instead of decorative, and it is the same split the codebase already drew between versioning a key and reconciling a shape. Errs toward more edge cases handled, which is your stated preference.

Completeness: 5A=10/10, 5B=7/10, 5C=5/10.

✅ Nightly and stable can share a session file and degrade gracefully in both directions, which matters because you ship three build identities side by side
✅ Turns a vague "be lenient" instinct into a rule a future contributor can follow without guessing
❌ The rule has to be honoured by hand forever; nothing enforces it, so a careless version bump still nukes sessions (human: ~15 min / CC: ~2 min)

options.label: 5B) Drop @Lossy, discard on any decode failure
options.description:
ELI10: Simplify. Any decode problem — one bad tab or a malformed file — discards the whole session and the app starts clean. No custom property wrapper, no per-element skipping.

Stakes if we pick wrong: one corrupted byte in one tab costs a user their entire multi-window layout, silently, on launch.

Completeness: 5B=7/10.

✅ Removes a hand-rolled decoding primitive and about 20 lines of the trickiest code in the change — unkeyed container walking is easy to get subtly wrong
✅ One failure rule instead of two makes the degradation table trivial to test exhaustively
❌ All-or-nothing on the launch path: the worst failure mode of the whole feature becomes its default response to any imperfection

options.label: 5C) Keep @Lossy, leave versioning undecided
options.description:
ELI10: Ship the wrapper as planned and decide the version-bump policy later, when someone actually adds a tab kind.

Stakes if we pick wrong: the decision gets made under pressure by whoever adds the kind, without the context that @Lossy exists to serve it.

Completeness: 5C=5/10.

✅ No decision needed now; the wrapper still protects against genuinely corrupt individual elements
❌ Leaves the feature's central robustness claim resting on an unwritten assumption, which is exactly how a load-bearing rationale gets lost

❌ All-or-nothing on the launch path: the worst failure mode of the whole feature becomes its default response to any imperfection

options.description:

Completeness: 5C=5/10.

✅ No decision needed now; the wrapper still protects against genuinely corrupt individual elements
❌ Leaves the feature's central robustness claim resting on an unwritten assumption, which is exactly how a load-bearing rationale gets lost

✅ Truly one home for the value; no precedence rule to explain, test, or get wrong later
✅ Removes a write from the selectedTargetID didSet, which is already a busy hot path doing four things
❌ Breaks the upgrade path unless a one-time migration reads the old key into a synthesised session, which is more code than keeping the fallback

options.description:

Stakes if we pick wrong: same two-writer ambiguity you just rejected for frames, in the value that decides which workroom the panels belong to.

Completeness: 6C=6/10.

✅ Zero diff, and the practical behaviour is right most of the time because the session file wins on restore
❌ Leaves a stale shadow value that looks authoritative to anyone reading DefaultsKeys.swift, and contradicts the decision just made for frames

## Section 3 — Test review

Framework from `CLAUDE.md` (authoritative): XCTest via `make app-test` (target `WorkroomAppTests`, `@testable import Workroom`), XCUITest via its own scheme. Go CLI untouched by this plan.

```
CODE PATHS                                                  USER FLOWS
[+] Core/SessionSnapshot.swift                              [+] Restore a session
  ├── LayoutNode.capture(address:)                            ├── [GAP] 2 windows quit → both back, right frames
  │   ├── [PLANNED ★★★] total map / drop+collapse / nil        ├── [GAP] panes+splits+focus land as left
  ├── LayoutNode.materialize(resolve:)                        └── [GAP] [→E2E] diff tab reopens on its file
  │   ├── [PLANNED ★★★] collapse / <2 leaves nil / bad orient
  │   └── [GAP]         ratio sanitize on hand-edited 0 or 1  [+] Save under load  ← REGRESSION (1A)
  ├── @Lossy decode                                           ├── [GAP] CRITICAL split while output streams,
  │   ├── [PLANNED ★★★] unknown kind drops 1, siblings live   │         force-quit → split survives
  │   └── [GAP]         same-version unknown kind (5A policy)  └── [GAP] digest guard: title churn ⇒ 0 writes
  ├── TabContent → TabSession (exhaustive switch)
  │   └── [PLANNED ★★★] run tab excluded, leaf collapses      [+] Cancelled quit  ← REGRESSION (2A)
  └── version gate newer / older / absent                     └── [GAP] CRITICAL ⌘Q → Cancel → keep working
      └── [PLANNED ★★]  discard, no migration yet                       → later edits still persist

[+] Core/SessionStore.swift                                 [+] Degradation
  ├── read: missing / unreadable / garbage / valid            ├── [GAP] corrupt file → 1 pane, no crash
  │   └── [PLANNED ★★★] + quarantine once                     ├── [GAP] deleted workroom → entry dropped
  ├── write atomic / writeSynchronously                       ├── [GAP] deleted file in a restored diff tab
  │   └── [PLANNED ★★★] no partial file                       │         → "unavailable", no crash
  └── bundle-id scoped path                                   └── [GAP] missing workroom dir → inert, no spawn
      └── [PLANNED ★★★] Dev ≠ Release
                                                            [+] Unchanged behaviour
[+] Core/AppStore+Session.swift                               ├── [GAP] fresh install → exactly 1 pane
  ├── dirty sink → debounce + MAX-DELAY (1A)                  ├── [GAP] ⌘N window still opens blank
  │   └── [GAP] CRITICAL forward progress under chatter       └── [GAP] What's New fires once, not per window
  ├── digest guard (WindowSession hash, savedAt outside)
  │   └── [PLANNED ★★]  pulse ⇒ equal snapshot ⇒ no write
  ├── flush: confirmed ⌘Q (2A) / SIGTERM / resignActive
  │   └── [GAP] CRITICAL freeze only past the cancel guard
  ├── restoreSession at end of apply(_:)
  │   └── [PLANNED ★★★] ensureInitialTerminal adds nothing

  ├── [PLANNED ★★★] order / split shape / focus / fresh ids
  ├── [PLANNED ★★★] dead cwd → target.path; no onFocusChange
```

questions.question: Issue 7 — how far should PR2's multi-window test coverage go? <gstack-qid:plan-eng-review-test-multiwindow-matrix>

options.label: 7A) Full matrix, unit + one XCUITest (recommended)
options.description:
ELI10: Cover every branch of window claiming as unit tests — the launch window adopting the first saved session, a sibling claiming its own by key, a ⌘N window claiming nothing, a key handed out twice being refused, and the What's-New guard firing once rather than once per restored window — plus the one XCUITest that proves two windows actually come back. Also test that a restored target whose workroom directory is gone stays inert and spawns no shell.

Stakes if we pick wrong: window claiming is the one part of this change with no user-visible symptom when it goes subtly wrong — a window silently adopts the wrong session's panels, or two windows race for one, and the only evidence is "my layout looks weird sometimes".

Recommendation: 7A — the claim logic is pure, main-actor, and dependency-light, so these are cheap unit tests, and the What's-New guard is exactly the kind of thing that ships broken and annoys every user on every launch. Matches your too-many-tests-rather-than-too-few preference.

Completeness: 7A=10/10, 7B=7/10, 7C=4/10.

✅ Every claim branch is a pure function over the loaded file, so the whole matrix is fast unit tests with no window lifecycle needed
✅ Catches the two silent failures — wrong-session adoption and N What's-New dialogs — that no user would report as a restore bug
❌ About six more test methods and one more XCUITest to maintain; the XCUITest needs a real GUI login session so it can't run headless (human: ~3h / CC: ~25 min)

options.label: 7B) Claim matrix only, skip the guards
options.description:
ELI10: Unit-test the claim branches and the two-window XCUITest, but skip the What's-New once-only guard and the missing-workroom inertness check.

Stakes if we pick wrong: a restored multi-window launch pops the What's New dialog once per window, which every user sees on the first launch after an update.

Completeness: 7B=7/10.

✅ Covers the logic most likely to be wrong — the claim branches — at the lowest test-maintenance cost
✅ Keeps the PR2 test suite small enough to read in one sitting
❌ Leaves two known-plausible failures untested, one of which is highly visible and arrives exactly when you least want it (right after an update)

options.label: 7C) One XCUITest, trust the rest
options.description:
ELI10: Ship a single end-to-end test that two windows come back, and rely on manual checking for the claim branches.

Stakes if we pick wrong: the claim edge cases — a stale key, a duplicate dispatch, a ⌘N window during restore — are exactly what an end-to-end happy-path test cannot see.

Completeness: 7C=4/10.

✅ Minimal test surface and the fastest path to landing PR2
❌ XCUITest is the slowest, flakiest layer in this repo and the least able to isolate which branch broke; the pure claim logic deserves unit tests precisely because it is pure

# Test Plan
Generated by /plan-eng-review on 2026-08-07
Branch: master
Repo: joelmoss/workroom
Feature: issue #46 — persist sessions (panels, layouts, windows)

## Affected Surfaces (macOS app — no web routes)
- App launch (cold start) — the restore path runs here; every failure is seen before the user can act.
- Terminal pane area (tab strip, split panes) — restored tabs, order, split geometry, focus.
- Window layer — number of windows reopened, their frames, which one is key.
- Changes / History inspectors — the source of restored diff, file, and changeset tabs.
- Quit paths — ⌘Q with and without the confirm dialog, and SIGTERM (`make app-run`, `pkill`).

## Key Interactions to Verify
- Split a pane (⌘D), quit, relaunch — the split comes back with no ⌘D.
- Open two or three tabs (⌘T), quit, relaunch — the same count, no stray "Terminal 1".
- Open a diff from the Changes panel and a changeset from History, quit, relaunch — both panes reopen.
- ⌘N a second window, arrange it differently, quit, relaunch — both windows return, each with its own
  frame, selection, and panes; the window that was key is key again.
- ⌘Q then Cancel, keep working, split a pane, quit properly — the last split is saved (not frozen out).
- Split a pane while a terminal is streaming output continuously, then force-quit — the split survives.

## Edge Cases
- Session file absent (fresh install) — exactly one pane, behaviour unchanged.
- Session file corrupt / truncated / garbage — app launches clean with one pane, no crash, no dialog.
- Session file from a newer build containing an unknown tab kind — that tab is dropped, siblings restore.
- A workroom in the session was deleted between launches — its entry drops, its split leaf collapses.
- A workroom directory is missing on disk — its tabs restore inertly, no shell is spawned.
- A restored diff points at a deleted file, or a changeset at a rebased-away commit — the pane shows
  its "unavailable" state rather than crashing or hanging.
- Run tabs are never restored — relaunch must not start a dev server.
- Workroom Dev and the release Workroom must not restore each other's sessions.

## Critical Paths
- Cold launch with a valid multi-window session → every window, frame, selection, tab, split, focus.
- Cold launch with no/corrupt session → single window, single terminal, no error surfaced.
- Quit → relaunch round trip with a busy terminal, proving saves happen under sustained output.
EOF

content.text:
## Section 4 — Performance review

No database, no N+1. Two things checked and cleared, one finding.

**Cleared:** restoring tab *models* is genuinely cheap — `GhosttySurfaceView.init` allocates an `NSView`, and the PTY plus Metal surface only appear in `createSurface()`, reachable from `viewDidMoveToWindow` / `ensureSurfaceCreated`. The codebase already banks on this (`AppStore.swift:2420-2423`: seeding N fixture targets *"costs N tab models and one terminal"*). **Cleared:** sibling windows at launch don't refork the CLI — `bootstrap` takes the `apply(projectStore.projects)` branch when the shared project list is already loaded.

**Issue 8 — `[P3] (confidence: 7/10)` the caps are too loose to be a real backstop.** The plan sets max 50 targets × 40 tabs per window × 8 windows. At the cap that's 16,000 tab models and unmounted `NSView`s allocated synchronously on the launch path. Medium confidence — realistic sessions are ~50 tabs and fine; this is about what the ceiling *permits*, not what you'd normally hit.

questions.question: Issue 8 — restore materialises every target's tabs eagerly at launch. Keep it, cap it tighter, or go lazy? <gstack-qid:plan-eng-review-perf-restore-caps>

options.label: 8A) Keep eager, tighten the caps (recommended)
options.description:
ELI10: Keep restoring every target's tabs at launch — it has to be eager, because the sidebar's terminal subtree and its restored expansion state render from those tabs, so a lazy target would show an empty or missing subtree until you clicked it. But bring the ceilings down to numbers you would actually be willing to allocate during launch: on the order of 20 targets and 20 tabs per window, with a log line naming what was dropped when a file exceeds them.

Stakes if we pick wrong: a pathological or hand-edited file makes the app allocate tens of thousands of views before the first frame, and the app appears hung on launch with no clue why.

Recommendation: 8A — eager is required for correct sidebar rendering, so the honest lever is the ceiling, and a cap nobody would accept in practice is not a backstop. The log line matters because the plan's own risk list already says silent truncation reads as full coverage.

Completeness: 8A=10/10, 8B=8/10, 8C=6/10.

✅ Preserves the restored sidebar expansion, which depends on those tabs existing before the sidebar renders
✅ Turns the caps from decoration into a real bound, and says out loud when they bite (human: ~20 min / CC: ~3 min)
❌ A user with a genuinely huge session silently loses the overflow; the log line is the only signal, and most users never read logs

options.label: 8B) Keep the plan's caps as written
options.description:
ELI10: Leave the ceilings at 50 targets, 40 tabs, 8 windows. They are a runaway backstop, not a target, and no real session approaches them.

Stakes if we pick wrong: only a corrupt or hand-edited file can reach the ceiling, and that file already gets you a slow launch rather than a wrong one.

Completeness: 8B=8/10.

✅ No further decisions or tuning; the numbers are generous enough that no legitimate user ever hits them
✅ Matches how NavigationHistory.maxEntries is used elsewhere in the codebase — a loose runaway guard, not a budget
❌ A ceiling that permits 16,000 view allocations on the launch path is not meaningfully bounding the worst case it exists to bound

options.label: 8C) Lazy per target
options.description:
ELI10: Keep the loaded session in memory and materialise a target's tabs the first time that target is selected, so launch allocates almost nothing.

Stakes if we pick wrong: the sidebar's restored terminal subtrees render empty until each workroom is visited, so the restore looks half-broken even though the data is there.

Completeness: 8C=6/10.

✅ Cheapest possible launch regardless of how large the saved session is
✅ Memory tracks what you actually use in a session rather than what you used last time
❌ Breaks restored sidebar expansion, adds a pending-materialisation state that every read path must know about, and reintroduces a race with ensureInitialTerminal on every first selection rather than just at launch
